#!/bin/bash

title: Week 8 — HPC & Reproducible Pipelines
section: 3 3. Snakemake: the pipeline as a DAG
text:
3 3. Snakemake: the pipeline as a DAG
Snakefile (shipped in the repo):
MODELS = ["ridge", "bayesb", "rf", "xgb"]
FOLDS  = range(1, 6)

rule all:
    input: "results/benchmark_report.html"

rule prep:
    output: "data/wheat_ready.rds"
    script: "R/prep_wheat.R"

rule cv_fold:
    input:  "data/wheat_ready.rds"
    output: "results/{model}_fold{fold}.rds"
    script: "R/run_fold_snake.R"

rule aggregate:
    input:  expand("results/{model}_fold{fold}.rds", model=MODELS, fold=FOLDS)
    output: "results/benchmark.csv"
    script: "R/aggregate.R"

rule report:
    input:  "results/benchmark.csv"
    output: "results/benchmark_report.html"
    shell:  "quarto render report/benchmark.qmd --output-dir ../results"
Snakemake infers the dependency graph from filenames, runs independent rules in parallel, and after a crash resumes exactly where it stopped. snakemake --executor slurm -j 25 dispatches rules as SLURM jobs.

title: Week 6 — Interactive Web Applications with Shiny
text:
1 1. Anatomy of a Shiny app
Two objects: a UI (layout + inputs/outputs) and a server (how outputs depend on inputs). Reactivity is a dependency graph — change input$trait and only downstream pieces recompute.
Three functions cover most needs: reactive() (shared computed value), render*() (outputs), observeEvent() (side-effects like downloads).

title: Week 6 — Interactive Web Applications with Shiny
section: 2 2. The course app: GWAS + GS explorer
text:
2 2. The course app: GWAS + GS explorer
Full source in shiny-app/app.R. Core skeleton:


Code
library(shiny); library(bslib); library(plotly); library(DT)

gwas <- readRDS("gwas_results.rds")   # trait, chr, pos, pvalue (Weeks 2–4 output)

ui <- page_sidebar(
  title = "Crop GWAS & GS Explorer — Sampath Perumal",
  sidebar = sidebar(
    selectInput("trait", "Trait", unique(gwas$trait)),
    sliderInput("thr", "-log10(p) threshold", 2, 10, 5, step = .5)
  ),
  card(card_header("Manhattan plot"), plotlyOutput("man")),
  card(card_header("Significant markers"), DTOutput("tbl"))
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  gw <- reactive(dplyr::filter(gwas, trait == input$trait))
  output$man <- renderPlotly({
    d <- gw()
    plot_ly(d, x = ~cum_pos, y = ~-log10(pvalue),
            color = ~factor(chr %% 2), colors = c("#159957", "#1e6bb8"),
            type = "scattergl", mode = "markers",
            text = ~marker, hoverinfo = "text+y") |>
      layout(showlegend = FALSE,
             shapes = list(list(type = "line", x0 = 0, x1 = max(d$cum_pos),
                                y0 = input$thr, y1 = input$thr,
                                line = list(dash = "dot"))))
  })
  output$tbl <- renderDT(dplyr::filter(gw(), -log10(pvalue) > input$thr))
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

title: Week 6 — Interactive Web Applications with Shiny
section: 3 3. Reactivity rules that prevent 90% of bugs
text:
3 3. Reactivity rules that prevent 90% of bugs

Compute once in a reactive(), use it in many outputs — never repeat filtering inside each render*().
No side-effects inside reactive(); those belong in observeEvent().
Big data: load once outside server, filter inside.

title: Week 4 — Machine Learning for Genomic Prediction
text:
flowchart LR
    A[Bias–variance<br/>tradeoff] --> B[Honest CV<br/>random vs grouped]
    B --> C[Penalized regression<br/>ridge=GBLUP · LASSO · enet]
    C --> D[Random Forest<br/>bagging + decorrelation]
    D --> E[Gradient boosting<br/>sequential residual fitting]
    E --> F[Benchmark table<br/>+ variable importance]
Datasets: BGLR::wheat (599 CIMMYT lines) and sommer::DT_technow (real maize hybrids, Technow et al. 2014) — wheat + a Canadian-relevant maize hybrid-prediction problem.

title: Week 4 — Machine Learning for Genomic Prediction
text:
1 1. Mechanics in plain language

Ridge (L2): shrink all coefficients; never zero. On markers, ridge regression is RR-BLUP is GBLUP — one model, three names. Memorize that identity.
LASSO (L1): shrink and select (some effects exactly zero). Struggles when SNPs are in LD — it picks one of a correlated set arbitrarily.
Elastic net: blend of both; the practical default for marker data.
Random forest: hundreds of trees, each on a bootstrap sample, each split limited to mtry random features. Averaging decorrelated trees slashes variance; out-of-bag samples give free validation; interactions/epistasis are captured without being specified.
Gradient boosting: trees fit sequentially to residuals of the ensemble so far; a small learning rate takes many careful steps. Strongest on tabular data, most tuning-sensitive.

title: Week 4 — Machine Learning for Genomic Prediction
text:
2 2. Honest cross-validation
Random k-fold leaks family information in structured populations — relatives end up in train and test, inflating accuracy. Use grouped CV (leave-family/environment-out) matched to deployment. Saying this unprompted is a senior-analyst signal.

title: Week 4 — Machine Learning for Genomic Prediction
text:
3 3. Benchmark on wheat


Code
library(tidyverse); library(glmnet); library(ranger); library(xgboost); library(BGLR)
data(wheat); X <- scale(wheat.X); y <- wheat.Y[,1]
set.seed(42); folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(y)))

bench <- map_dfr(1:5, function(k) {
  tr <- folds != k; te <- !tr
  # ridge & lasso (CV-tuned lambda inside training folds only)
  rid <- cv.glmnet(X[tr,], y[tr], alpha = 0)
  las <- cv.glmnet(X[tr,], y[tr], alpha = 1)
  # random forest
  rf  <- ranger(y = y[tr], x = as.data.frame(X[tr,]), num.trees = 500, seed = 1)
  # xgboost
  xgb <- xgboost(data = X[tr,], label = y[tr], nrounds = 300, eta = 0.05,
                 max_depth = 4, subsample = .8, verbose = 0)
  tibble(fold = k,
    Ridge  = cor(predict(rid, X[te,], s = "lambda.min"), y[te]),
    LASSO  = cor(predict(las, X[te,], s = "lambda.min"), y[te]),
    RF     = cor(predict(rf, as.data.frame(X[te,]))$predictions, y[te]),
    XGB    = cor(predict(xgb, X[te,]), y[te]))
})
bench |> summarise(across(-fold, \(x) round(mean(x), 3)))


# A tibble: 1 × 4
  Ridge LASSO    RF   XGB
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 0.526 0.476 0.575 0.578


Typical outcome: ridge ≈ or > the fancy learners on polygenic yield. Additive, small-effect traits are ridge’s home turf — the honest conclusion most papers bury.

title: Week 4 — Machine Learning for Genomic Prediction
text:
4 4. Which markers drive the forest?


Code
rf_all <- ranger(y = y, x = as.data.frame(X), num.trees = 800,
                 importance = "permutation", seed = 1)
enframe(sort(rf_all$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE)[1:20]) |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(name, value), value)) + geom_col(fill = "#159957") +
  coord_flip() + theme_minimal() + labs(x = NULL, y = "Permutation importance")









Compare these to single-marker GWAS hits — overlap validates; RF-only hits hint at interactions.

title: Week 2 — Multivariate Statistics & Dimension Reduction
text:
flowchart LR
    A[Scaling &<br/>distance] --> B[PCA<br/>structure & QC]
    B --> C[Clustering<br/>k-means · hierarchical · mclust]
    C --> D[sPLS-DA<br/>supervised, sparse]
    D --> E[Validation<br/>permutation · CV]
Dataset: agridat::gauch.soy multi-environment soybean for PCA-of-GxE, plus a built-in genomic marker matrix from sommer::DT_cpdata (real 363-line apple-progeny SNP data) standing in for a pea/canola panel — swap in your own VCF-derived matrix with one line.

title: Week 2 — Multivariate Statistics & Dimension Reduction
text:
1 1. PCA — what it actually does
PCA eigen-decomposes the covariance matrix: PC1 is the direction of maximum variance, PC2 the next, orthogonal. On a marker matrix, leading PCs approximate ancestry — the population structure you correct for in GWAS.


Code
library(tidyverse); library(sommer); library(factoextra)
data(DT_cpdata)                 # DT = pheno, GT = markers (-1/0/1)
M <- GT_cpdata
p <- prcomp(M, scale. = TRUE)
fviz_eig(p, addlabels = TRUE, ncp = 8)











Code
scores <- as_tibble(p$x[,1:2]) |> mutate(color = DT_cpdata$color)
ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = color)) + geom_point(alpha = .7) +
  theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Genetic structure from SNPs")















Tip



Swap in your crop: M <- vcfR::extract.gt(...) → numeric matrix → identical workflow for a pea or canola panel.

title: Week 2 — Multivariate Statistics & Dimension Reduction
section: 2 2. How many groups? Clustering with validation
text:
2 2. How many groups? Clustering with validation


Code
library(mclust)
km  <- kmeans(p$x[,1:5], centers = 3, nstart = 25)
mc  <- Mclust(p$x[,1:5], G = 1:6)     # model-based; picks G by BIC
mc$G


[1] 1


Code
fviz_cluster(km, data = p$x[,1:2], geom = "point") + theme_minimal()









k-means needs k chosen; mclust fits Gaussian mixtures and lets BIC choose. Report silhouette or BIC, never just a pretty plot.

title: Week 2 — Multivariate Statistics & Dimension Reduction
text:
3 3. Supervised: sparse PLS-DA
PCA ignores labels. PLS-DA finds components that separate known groups; the sparse version selects a small marker/metabolite panel — interpretable and directly useful for assay design.


Code
library(mixOmics)
Y <- factor(km$cluster)                     # demo labels; use market class/origin in practice
res <- splsda(M, Y, ncomp = 2, keepX = c(30, 20))
plotIndiv(res, ellipse = TRUE, legend = TRUE, title = "sPLS-DA")









Honest validation — mandatory:


Code
perf(res, validation = "Mfold", folds = 5, nrepeat = 20)   # error rates
# + permutation test: shuffle Y, refit — separation should collapse


sPLS-DA will happily “separate” random labels; permutation testing is what keeps you honest (a favourite interview probe).

title: Week 2 — Multivariate Statistics & Dimension Reduction
section: 4 4. GxE with PCA: the AMMI idea
text:
4 4. GxE with PCA: the AMMI idea


Code
library(agridat); data(gauch.soy)
gxe <- gauch.soy |> group_by(gen, env) |> summarise(y = mean(yield), .groups="drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = env, values_from = y) |> column_to_rownames("gen")
gxe_c <- sweep(sweep(as.matrix(gxe), 1, rowMeans(gxe)), 2, colMeans(gxe)) + mean(as.matrix(gxe))
pg <- prcomp(gxe_c)
fviz_pca_biplot(pg, repel = TRUE, geom = "point", title = "AMMI-style GxE biplot")









Genotypes near the origin are stable; those aligned with an environment vector are specifically adapted — the statistical heart of MET interpretation.

title: Week 0a — Biostatistics Primer
text:
1 What biostatistics is
Biostatistics is the science of learning from biological data in the presence of variation. Two plants of the same genotype never yield identically — the job is to separate signal (genetics, treatment) from noise (environment, measurement) and to state honestly how sure we are.

title: Week 0a — Biostatistics Primer
text:
2 Populations, samples, and estimation

Population: every canola plant that could ever be grown from a cultivar.
Sample: the 200 plots you actually harvested.
Parameter (unknown truth, e.g. true mean yield μ) vs estimate (your sample mean x̄).

Statistical inference quantifies how far x̄ may sit from μ.

title: Week 0a — Biostatistics Primer
text:
3 Distributions you will meet constantly


Code
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)
d <- bind_rows(
  tibble(x = rnorm(4000, 40, 6),        dist = "Normal — yield (bu/ac)"),
  tibble(x = rbinom(4000, 10, .3),      dist = "Binomial — diseased plants /10"),
  tibble(x = rnbinom(4000, mu = 20, size = 2), dist = "Neg. binomial — RNA-seq counts")
)
ggplot(d, aes(x)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#159957") +
  facet_wrap(~dist, scales = "free") + theme_minimal()

















Distribution
Crop example
Model family




Normal
yield, height, oil %
linear model


Binomial
disease incidence
logistic GLM


Poisson / Negative binomial
counts; RNA-seq reads
count GLM (NB handles overdispersion)

title: Week 0a — Biostatistics Primer
text:
4 Hypothesis testing in five sentences

State a null H₀ (e.g., “no yield difference between lines”).
Compute a test statistic from the data.
The p-value = probability of a statistic at least this extreme if H₀ were true. It is not the probability H₀ is true.
Type I error (α): rejecting a true H₀ — false positive. Type II (β): missing a real effect. Power = 1 − β, driven by replication, effect size, and noise.
A tiny p with a trivial effect size is not a finding — always report effect sizes.



Code
t.test(extra ~ group, data = sleep)   # classic built-in example



    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  extra by group
t = -1.8608, df = 17.776, p-value = 0.07939
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 1 and group 2 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -3.3654832  0.2054832
sample estimates:
mean in group 1 mean in group 2 
           0.75            2.33

title: Week 0a — Biostatistics Primer
text:
5 Confidence intervals
A 95% CI is the set of parameter values compatible with the data: across repeated experiments, 95% of such intervals capture the truth. Prefer CIs to bare p-values — they show magnitude and uncertainty.

title: Week 0a — Biostatistics Primer
section: 6 Experimental design — where good statistics starts
text:
6 Experimental design — where good statistics starts

Replication — quantifies noise; no reps, no inference.
Randomization — protects against hidden bias (soil gradients).
Blocking — put comparisons close together: RCBD, alpha-lattice, row–column designs used in every serious yield trial. Week 1 models these directly.

title: Week 0a — Biostatistics Primer
text:
7 Why multiple testing matters (GWAS preview)
Test 1 SNP at α = 0.05 → 5% false-positive risk. Test 500,000 SNPs → ~25,000 false positives expected under the null. Week 2–3 pages use Bonferroni and FDR to fix this.

title: Week 0a — Biostatistics Primer
text:
8 Exercises

Simulate 1,000 t-tests under the null (rnorm both groups). What fraction have p < 0.05? Why?
For a trait with σ = 5 and a true difference of 2, use power.t.test() to find n per group for 80% power.
Sketch (on paper) an RCBD for 20 lines, 3 blocks, on a field with a known fertility gradient.

title: Applied Biostatistics & Machine Learning for Crop Genomics
text:
This course teaches the statistical foundations behind modern crop genomics — mixed models, multivariate statistics, Bayesian inference, machine learning, multi-omics integration — and the delivery skills that turn analysis into tools: interactive web apps, databases, and HPC pipelines.
Every module runs on real, public datasets from crops that matter to Canadian agriculture: prairie yield trials, CIMMYT wheat, pea diversity panels, canola RNA-seq, and maize hybrids.






Who this is for



Bioinformaticians and geneticists who use statistics daily and want to understand how the methods actually work — and statisticians who want realistic genomic case studies.

Code
# Binomial GLM: disease incidence example (simulated scores on real structure)
set.seed(2)
oats$diseased <- rbinom(nrow(oats), 10, plogis(-1 + 0.02 * scale(oats$yield)))
glm1 <- glm(cbind(diseased, 10 - diseased) ~ gen, family = binomial, data = oats)
summary(glm1)$coefficients |> head(3)

(Intercept)   -0.99039870  0.1452546 -6.8183638 9.208319e-12

title: Week 1 — Linear & Mixed Models
section: 3 3. The mixed model: y = Xβ + Zu + e
text:
3 3. The mixed model: y = Xβ + Zu + e
Blocks and genotypes become random effects: they share a distribution, so estimates borrow strength and shrink toward the mean.


Code
mm1 <- lmer(yield ~ factor(nitro) + (1 | gen) + (1 | block), data = oats)
summary(mm1)$varcor


 Groups   Name        Std.Dev.
 block    (Intercept) 15.6540 
 gen      (Intercept)  5.2388 
 Residual             15.3130 


Heritability from variance components (line-mean basis):


Code
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mm1))
Vg <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "gen"]; Ve <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]
h2 <- Vg / (Vg + Ve / 3)        # 3 blocks
round(h2, 2)


[1] 0.26


BLUP shrinkage, visualized:


Code
re <- ranef(mm1)$gen; blup <- setNames(re[,1], rownames(re))
blue <- coef(lm(yield ~ gen - 1, oats)) - mean(oats$yield)
tibble(line = names(blup), BLUE = as.numeric(blue)[seq_along(blup)], BLUP = as.numeric(blup)) |>
  pivot_longer(-line) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, line, colour = name)) + geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Deviation from mean", colour = NULL) + theme_minimal()









BLUPs sit closer to zero — shrinkage in proportion to reliability. This is what genomic BLUP does with markers.

data(gilmour.serpentine)

c(base = m_base$AIC, spatial = m_spat$AIC)

331.0000 294.9681

5 Interview-grade summary

Random vs fixed: “Random effects share a distribution; I model genotypes as random to get shrunken BLUPs and variance components for heritability.”
Spatial: “AR1×AR1 or 2-D splines model field trend; ignoring it inflates error and mis-ranks lines.”

title: Week 3 — Bayesian Inference & Genomic Prediction
text:
flowchart LR
    A[Bayes theorem<br/>prior × likelihood] --> B[MCMC<br/>Gibbs sampling]
    B --> C[Diagnostics<br/>trace · R-hat · ESS]
    C --> D[Bayesian alphabet<br/>BRR · BayesA/B/C · BL]
    D --> E[Cross-validated<br/>prediction accuracy]
Dataset: BGLR::wheat — 599 CIMMYT wheat lines, 1,279 DArT markers, grain yield in 4 environments (Crossa et al. 2010). The benchmark genomic-selection dataset.

title: Week 3 — Bayesian Inference & Genomic Prediction
text:
1 1. Bayes in one paragraph
Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. Priors are regularization with a probability interpretation: a Normal prior on marker effects is ridge/GBLUP; a Laplace prior is the LASSO; mixture priors (BayesB/C) say “most markers do nothing.” With n ≪ p, the prior is not optional — every GS method is a prior choice.

title: Week 3 — Bayesian Inference & Genomic Prediction
text:
2 2. Load the classic data


Code
library(BGLR); library(tidyverse); library(coda)
data(wheat)
X <- scale(wheat.X)          # 599 x 1279 markers
y <- wheat.Y[, 1]            # yield, environment 1
dim(X)


[1]  599 1279

title: Week 3 — Bayesian Inference & Genomic Prediction
text:
3 3. Fit Bayesian Ridge and BayesB


Code
set.seed(7)
dir.create("bglr_tmp", showWarnings = FALSE)
fit_brr <- BGLR(y = y, ETA = list(mrk = list(X = X, model = "BRR")),
                nIter = 6000, burnIn = 1000, saveAt = "bglr_tmp/brr_", verbose = FALSE)
fit_bb  <- BGLR(y = y, ETA = list(mrk = list(X = X, model = "BayesB")),
                nIter = 6000, burnIn = 1000, saveAt = "bglr_tmp/bb_",  verbose = FALSE)


(6k iterations keeps the page fast; use 30k+ with 5k burn-in for real work.)

Code

Code

    var1 
566.9967 


A “fuzzy caterpillar” trace, effective sample size in the hundreds, and (with multiple chains) R-hat ≈ 1.00 — say these three things in an interview and you’ve answered the MCMC question.

section: 5 5. Where the models disagree: marker effects
text:
5 5. Where the models disagree: marker effects


Code
tibble(marker = 1:ncol(X),
       BRR    = abs(fit_brr$ETA$mrk$b),
       BayesB = abs(fit_bb$ETA$mrk$b)) |>
  pivot_longer(-marker) |>
  ggplot(aes(marker, value)) + geom_point(size = .4, alpha = .5) +
  facet_wrap(~name) + theme_minimal() +
  labs(y = "|marker effect|", title = "Shrink-everything vs select-few priors")









BRR spreads small effects everywhere; BayesB concentrates signal — matching infinitesimal vs oligogenic architectures.

title: Week 3 — Bayesian Inference & Genomic Prediction
section: 6 6. The only score that matters: predictive ability
text:
6 6. The only score that matters: predictive ability


Code
set.seed(42)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(y)))
acc <- map_dfr(1:5, function(k) {
  yNA <- y; yNA[folds == k] <- NA
  f1 <- BGLR(yNA, ETA = list(m = list(X = X, model = "BRR")),
             nIter = 6000, burnIn = 1000, saveAt = "bglr_tmp/cv1_", verbose = FALSE)
  f2 <- BGLR(yNA, ETA = list(m = list(X = X, model = "BayesB")),
             nIter = 6000, burnIn = 1000, saveAt = "bglr_tmp/cv2_", verbose = FALSE)
  tibble(fold = k,
         BRR    = cor(f1$yHat[folds == k], y[folds == k]),
         BayesB = cor(f2$yHat[folds == k], y[folds == k]))
})




Code
acc |> summarise(across(BRR:BayesB, mean)) |> round(3)


# A tibble: 1 × 2
    BRR BayesB
  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 0.526  0.518


On polygenic wheat yield the two typically tie — that result is the lesson: architecture determines the winner, so benchmark on your trait, don’t assume.

title: Week 5 — RNA-seq & Multi-Omics Integration
text:
flowchart LR
    A[Counts → NB GLM<br/>DESeq2] --> B[Multiple testing<br/>FDR]
    B --> C[WGCNA<br/>modules & eigengenes]
    C --> D[MOFA2<br/>factors across omics]
    D --> E[Biomarkers &<br/>interpretation]
Data: a downsampled real Brassica napus RNA-seq count matrix (via data/get_data.R, pulled from NCBI GEO) with a simulated-but-realistic methylation layer for the integration demo — swap in your own matrices with two lines.

title: Week 5 — RNA-seq & Multi-Omics Integration
text:
1 1. Why counts need negative binomial
RNA-seq counts are overdispersed (variance > mean): Poisson understates noise → false positives. DESeq2 models counts ~ NB, shrinks per-gene dispersions toward a trend (empirical Bayes — Week 3’s idea reappearing), and tests log-fold-changes with a Wald or LRT test. The design formula is Week 1’s linear model: ~ batch + condition.


Code
library(DESeq2)
counts <- readRDS("data/bnapus_counts.rds")     # genes x samples
meta   <- readRDS("data/bnapus_meta.rds")       # condition, batch
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(counts, meta, design = ~ batch + condition)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)




Code
# Self-contained demo so the page always renders: simulate NB counts w/ signal
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(9)
n_g <- 2000; de <- 1:150
mu  <- rexp(n_g, 1/200)
cts <- sapply(1:6, \(i) rnbinom(n_g, mu = mu * ifelse(i > 3 & seq_len(n_g) %in% de, 2, 1), size = 3))
pv  <- apply(cts, 1, \(x) wilcox.test(x[1:3], x[4:6])$p.value)
padj <- p.adjust(pv, "BH")
tibble(gene = 1:n_g, padj, truly_DE = gene %in% de) |>
  count(sig = padj < .05, truly_DE)


# A tibble: 3 × 3
  sig   truly_DE     n
  <lgl> <lgl>    <int>
1 FALSE FALSE     1849
2 FALSE TRUE       150
3 NA    FALSE        1


FDR (Benjamini–Hochberg) controls the proportion of false discoveries — with 20k genes, the right currency. Bonferroni controls any single false positive and is appropriate for GWAS-style confirmatory claims.

title: Week 5 — RNA-seq & Multi-Omics Integration
text:
2 2. Co-expression: WGCNA in concept
Correlation matrix → soft-threshold power (approximate scale-free topology) → topological overlap → hierarchical modules → module eigengene (first PC of the module) → correlate eigengenes with traits. It’s Week 2’s PCA working inside a network.


Code
library(WGCNA)
sft <- pickSoftThreshold(t(vst_counts))
net <- blockwiseModules(t(vst_counts), power = sft$powerEstimate, minModuleSize = 30)
moduleTraitCor <- cor(net$MEs, traits)

title: Week 5 — RNA-seq & Multi-Omics Integration
section: 3 3. MOFA2: one factor model across omics layers
text:
3 3. MOFA2: one factor model across omics layers
MOFA2 = factor analysis across matched RNA-seq + methylation (+ genotype PAV) matrices: latent factors capture shared variation, with per-layer variance-explained telling you which omics drives which factor. Unsupervised, handles missing layers, the modern default.


Code
library(MOFA2)
mofa <- create_mofa(list(RNA = rna_mat, Methylation = meth_mat))
mofa <- prepare_mofa(mofa, model_options = get_default_model_options(mofa))
mofa <- run_mofa(mofa, use_basilisk = TRUE)
plot_variance_explained(mofa)
plot_top_weights(mofa, view = "RNA", factor = 1, nfeatures = 15)


Supervised counterpart: DIABLO (mixOmics::block.splsda) when you have groups to discriminate and want a cross-omics biomarker panel.

title: Week 5 — RNA-seq & Multi-Omics Integration
section: 4 4. The three questions to ask any omics analysis
text:
4 4. The three questions to ask any omics analysis

Is the design confounded (batch ⟂ condition)? Check before modeling; fix with design terms or ComBat/RUV.
Is the test matched to the distribution (NB for counts, logit-M for methylation proportions)?
Is multiplicity controlled, and is FDR the right currency for the claim?

Credits: DESeq2 (Love et al. 2014), WGCNA (Langfelder & Horvath 2008), MOFA2 (Argelaguet et al. 2020).

title: Week 7 — Databases & APIs for Breeding Data
section: 5 5. Serve it: a REST API in 20 lines
text:
5 5. Serve it: a REST API in 20 lines
api/plumber.R:


Code
library(plumber); library(DBI); library(RSQLite)

#* @apiTitle Breeding data API — Sampath Perumal

#* Mean phenotype by family
#* @param trait Trait name
#* @get /summary
function(trait = "Yield") {
  con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), "course.db"); on.exit(dbDisconnect(con))
  dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT l.family, AVG(p.value) AS mean_val
                   FROM phenotypes p JOIN lines l USING(line_id)
                   WHERE p.trait = ? GROUP BY l.family", params = list(trait))
}


Run: plumber::plumb("api/plumber.R")$run(port = 8000) → http://localhost:8000/summary?trait=Oil returns JSON. Your Week 6 Shiny app, a Python script, and a collaborator’s browser all consume the same endpoint — that’s the architecture sentence worth saying in interviews.
